Thank you. There was another point which the hon. member made this afternoon and which I think calls for some comment. As I announced in this house in late September, I think, we held a conference in Halifax-it was referred to as a symposium-attended not only by several provincial ministers and some deputies but by more than 50 municipal representatives. We discussed the amendments to the act and the possibilities under the new legislation When we convened not only the Halifax conference but the subsequent conference in St. John's I was acting, upon a suggestion which was made here in the house by one of the Toronto members, I think it was the hon. member for Danforth, who in the course

of his remarks on the amendments to the National Housing Act said he had a few constructive suggestions to make and offered the hope that at a later date they would be given attention. But in the main he was most complimentary about the program envisaged by this new act. He went on to make it clear, however, that in the absence of active co-operation and enthusiastic support from provincial and municipal governments this new act, of which I think we can all be very proud, would be meaningless. And he suggested a series of these conferences. The object was to ensure that every municipality in Canada or that every province in Canada would know of the possibilities and of the facilities which are now available under the new legislation. That was the purpose of these meetings.
The Halifax meeting was attended not only by the president of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but by all of the directors of the board with one exception. The vice president and other senior officials also were there, as were the members of parliament for that riding and some members of the legislature. Questions were answered and there was a really worth-while discussion. I think I can say the conference was a great success. Then on October 8, 9, and 10 I visited Newfoundland in company with the president, the vice president and other senior officials of C.M.H.C. There we found the premier together with several other ministers of the Newfoundland government in attendance with the deputy ministers and officials concerned. No fewer than 75 municipal representatives came to St. John's for this two-day symposium. I think it was a timely and helpful discussion. I will go further and say it was a very lively discussion- you cannot spend two days in Newfoundland without things being lively, especially when a question period is included.
We have arranged for meetings in Alberta on November 5 and 6. The meeting on November 5 will be held in Calgary and the meeting on November 6 in Lethbridge, while the federation of municipalities of the province of Alberta is holding its annual meeting. At the request of the federation we are holding the meeting at the same time. The provincial minister and I will be in attendance, along with the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on that occasion. Not only will the subject of housing generally be under discussion but the possibilities of using the new act for sewerage construction projects and, more particularly the advantages of an
Supply-National Revenue extensive program of urban renewal, will be discussed at length during that meeting.
I welcome this opportunity to make an announcement. A few weeks ago, I stated that the two provincial ministers concerned and
I	had agreed on the dates for the housing conference for eastern and southern Ontario as November 23 and 24, in Toronto. I have since found we were not able to get sufficient hotel accommodation for those dates. I also found that not only the mayor of Ottawa but the mayor of London, Ontario, and the mayor of Toronto felt it would be better to wait until after the municipal elections. This morning, with the assurance of the provincial ministers that they were in agreement, we changed the dates to December 16 and 17 by which time the elections will be over and some thought will have been given to who will be the leaders of housing programs by all the mayors and the reeves. So the meetings will be held in Toronto on December 16 and 17. The federation of mayors and reeves have been advised and are in agreement with the new dates.
Now I should like to make a special reference to the Fraserview veterans' housing project which, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has said, has been the subject of many questions. A series of questions has been asked in the house relating to the increases in rents which were introduced effective October 1 of this year. This housing project comprises 1,146 houses. They are units of two, three and four bedrooms. This is one of several projects completed after world war
II	under the 1948 and 1949 veterans' rental housing program. Hon. members may recall the statements which were made in answer to questions raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East and other hon. members. Approximately 12,000 houses were built across Canada during the two years which followed the passing of the legislation. All of them were rented to veterans of the second world war and of the Korean war.
I should like to make it clear-and this is apparent from the discussion which took place when the original legislation was passed-that this project was not intended to provide subsidized housing for veterans. It was intended to provide badly needed houses at fair rentals for veterans of the second world war and of the Korean campaign in large parts of Canada where the need arose. In 1954 it became apparent that the demand for rental accommodation for veterans was diminishing and that in most cities it was over. In that year the government of the day

Supply-National Revenue authorized the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to offer houses for sale to qualified veterans. However, before the houses could be placed on sale certain requirements had to be met. In the first place the corporation had obtained the co-operation of several cities and other municipalities in providing sites for the houses, and renegotiation with these municipalities had to take place. In addition an assurance had to be received from veterans' organizations and others that there was no longer an acute shortage in a particular city or municipality and that there would be sufficient demand from veterans to buy these houses if they were offered for sale, I might say that when they were initially offered for sale, the sale price of these houses was established on a national basis. But in setting prices for each individual project consideration was given to a series of factors, including the original cost of construction, the age and condition of the houses, their location and their fair market value at the time they were offered for sale. The government was to try, if this could be done in a reasonable way, to recover its full outlay in respect of these houses on a national basis. This policy resulted in sale prices which were somewhat higher than the actual cost in some communities where the market values were higher, and in prices which were somewhat lower in a number of communities where market values were lower. This policy enabled Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the instrument of the government concerned, to offer houses for sale in individual communities in the light of existing conditions there.
Because market values in Nova Scotia are quite different from market values in Ontario or British Columbia, you have higher prices in one place than in another. That is not surprising. But if you had sold a house in Vancouver that had gone up in value by $3,000 or $4,000, you would have upset the market conditions in that area and you would in effect have been bonusing, to the detriment of taxpayers, including other veterans, all projects in other parts of the country. It was felt they should not offer houses for sale in any city or town at prices likely to disrupt the market too radically.
There was also a serious objection to this program based on the fact that there would be serious speculation in some cities. Houses that might have cost $10,000 or $12,000 in 1949 or 1950 had in some instances appreciated in value, due to conditions in that particular city, by as much as $4,000 or $5,000.

It was agreed that if a veteran wanted to buy a house, to prevent speculation they would add right across Canada the sum of $1,000 per house, which was to be written off if the veteran remained in the house for a five-year period. It was to be written off at so much a year for five years. This technique, I might say, was known as the rebate procedure. I am assured, not only by the officials of central mortgage and housing but by veterans and others that this procedure has worked successfully in connection with projects in many parts of Canada.
Although the agreement with the city of Vancouver covering Fraserview was successfully renegotiated in 1955 to permit the sales program, they were not able to embark on sales immediately because final construction costs for the whole project were not known at that time. The Fraserview project was therefore the last one of the 10 or 15 or more projects throughout Canada that went on the market. The cost reports were completed by the end of 1958, and in February, 1959, the representatives of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation met with more than 500 of the Fraserview tenants and presented a schedule of proposed prices, together with terms of sale, and that schedule included this $1,000 mark-up which would be rebated if the veteran held the house for a five year period.
The meeting was in February, 1959, and there was almost unanimous acceptance of this schedule. The houses were offered for sale on May 1, 1959. I might say that the records show beyond a shadow of a doubt that the fair value of the average housing unit in Fraserview was $2,000 to $4,000 per unit higher than the actual cost at that time. If they had been sold, it would have meant that every veteran in those houses, in addition to the other benefits he had received would have received a bonus of at least $1,000, because the $1,000 rebate would come into the picture if he had sold the house after a five year period.
Throughout this whole program of disposing of houses-this practice has been followed consistently in most parts of Canada- Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have disposed of thousands of these units under this program. In Vancouver, up to the beginning of June of this year, they had disposed of over 500 houses of the 1,140 or so that comprised this project. But during the whole of this period in every city or community in Canada that had a program of this kind semi-annual reviews were carried on

to determine whether the $1,000 rebate procedure should be retained in different cities. The corporation, through its staff and advisers, were also kept aware of market conditions not only in Vancouver but in other cities. In May, 1963, to encourage the sale of the Fraserview houses to veterans, a team of corporation appraisers was appointed specially to look into the Fraserview situation. They recommended the removal of the rebate. This is not surprising, because the five year period had elapsed, even in the case of British Columbia, in the period 1954 to 1959. They also recommended a reduction of $600 in the sale price of basementless houses.
But I would point out that in the same report that was made in the late spring of 1963 it was shown that existing rents were substantially below the level of houses of that quality in that part of Vancouver. On July 25, 1963, the $1,000 rebate was removed from the sale of these houses and the prices of the basementless units were reduced by the $600 recommended by the corporation's appraisers. However, at the same time the corporation announced rent increases ranging from $3.50 to $11.50 per month to take effect on September 1, 1963. Following this representations were made on behalf of the tenants by several people, including the hon. member for Vancouver South. I believe representations were also made by the hon. member for Vancouver East, but I know they were made by the hon. member for Vancouver South. As a result of representations from several sources, the rent increases were deferred and the minister then in charge, the late Jack Garland, after consulting with the corporation and receiving their agreement in this regard, arranged for an independent appraisal to be carried out with regard to the rentals that should be charged and as to the values of these houses.
The appraisal company that was brought in was Bell-Irving Realty Limited, of Vancouver, the president of which is a distinguished veteran, Brigadier Henry P. Bell-Irving. He has a distinguished war record; he was awarded the D.S.O. and O.B.E., and fought in Italy and on the western front. The firm's appraiser, Mr. E. W. Palmer, was eminently qualified for the task he was asked to perform. He is an accredited appraiser of the appraisal institute of Canada, a senior real estate appraiser in the society of real estate appraisers, a fellow of the valuers institute of London, England, and a member
Supply-National Revenue of the professional division of the realtors institute of British Columbia. He is considered by all who know him to be a highly qualified specialist in this field.
The Bell-Irving appraisal confirmed the corporation's report of May, 1963, but recommended that further reductions should be made in the sale prices of two basic house types in the amounts of $300 and $500. The corporation immediately implemented the reductions recommended by this independent appraiser; they were implemented on June 1, 1964, and since that time I understand that another 50 or so houses have been sold. The effect of these adjustments was to establish selling prices that are in the order of $500 to $600 below current market values in Vancouver. I ask the hon. member for Vancouver East to keep that in mind. This shows conclusively that the prices at which veterans are now able to buy them are in the order of $500 to $600 a house lower than the current market value for that type of house. At the time these reductions were effected the corporation's board of directors reaffirmed the previously recommended rent increases that should have taken effect in September, 1963. They reaffirmed them to take effect on October 1, 1964. In June last notices to that effect were sent out to the 601 tenants. They were given until September 15 to signify whether they wanted to enter into a new lease at the increased rents. I might say that the increase in rentals is due largely if not entirely to an increase in grants in lieu of taxes being paid to the city of Vancouver. There is no profit in it for the corporation. The increases do not cover the added amount paid on the Fraserview houses to the municipality. These rent increases range from $3.50 to $11 per month.
By the deadline of September 15, 419 of the 601 tenants had accepted, 38 had purchased their houses, 12 had vacated, leaving 132 not heard from. In the two weeks which followed, that is between September 15 and October 1, 59 more tenants made their decision and as of the close of business on September 30 the corporation then had 73 tenants from whom they had not heard. The corporation then sent out notices that since the tenants had not entered into these new arrangements they would be evicted. Of course this would not mean that if they had a good case they would be evicted; a judge of the court would listen to the reasons in any case coming before him. I have stated repeatedly that since this matter had been reduced to manageable proportions I was quite prepared to have the officials of the

Supply-National Revenue department consider each individual case, or if anyone wanted to take them up with me individually I would be pleased to do so.

Could I ask the minister a question. Could he tell the committee on what basis the appraisers set these rents? Was it on the basis of actual cost or a rent which would retire the investment which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has made, plus current expenses, or was it a rent which was based on current rents in the area?

The rents in all cases are lower than rents in the area for houses of similar value. The combination of circumstances to which I referred-the cost of the house, its condition and other factors-were all taken into consideration, as well as general rents in the area.

The minister is talking about the condition of the houses and I assume is talking about the sale price; but in determining these rents was the determination based solely on an economic rental to cover the investment of C.M.H.C. or was any other factor taken into consideration?

The rents were just enough to carry these houses, but not to make any profit out of the transaction. They are amortized to the amount of the balance owing so as to pay current taxes and maintenance and operating expenses.
Could the minister tell me at what rate was the amortization?
The amortization was on the basis of 2J per cent interest over a period of 50 years, credit being given for the amount which had accumulated up to that date.
Might I ask whether in this compilation the amount which had been cleared off through depreciation over the years was also taken into consideration?

Might I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that I be allowed to finish my statement. I have had prepared a table which will help answer these questions, and then if hon. members have any further questions I will do my best today to answer them.
As of the close of business on September 30 there were some 73 people who had not agreed to enter into new leases; two of the people who said they were going to did not in fact do so. Then in the two weeks which followed the notices of eviction which were sent out, certain other people indicated that


they wanted to stay on in the houses. This reduced the total of 73 to a total of 54 by a date in early October.
Yesterday I received from 18 other people -that is in addition to the 52 plus the two -altogether 54-signed letters addressed to me which obviously had been typed by the same machine, indicating an organized drive. These letters asked for a public hearing. All but 54 of these 600 odd tenants are paying the new rents and have paid them for the month of October. So that while over 500 people out of the 601 have entered into some new leasing arrangement, another dozen or more have vacated voluntarily and I think about 40 people have bought houses, you have at the outside, taking the 52 and 18, 70 people who are still complaining. These people have had the benefit of the lower rentals for more than a year. The corporation has not collected rents so as to carry this project for over a year. The corporation's appraisers recommended that these rent increases should take effect last summer. Further delay will be unfair to the people who have bought houses, and the 500 odd people who have entered into the new leases and are paying them without complaint. I am not saying that there are not people who do not complain. Of course, no one likes to have his rent raised and any one of us would complain of that. But many veterans have stated publicly that they do not want to be subsidized in these houses and are willing to pay, which is demonstrated by the fact that over 500 of them are paying the higher rents.
To explain the current rents and also the current selling prices I have had a tabulation prepared showing the individual type of houses and listing the original selling price, that is, the price at which these houses were offered in 1959 and which was almost unanimously accepted by the tenants. On the same sheet is shown the adjusted price as a result of the corporation's appraisal in 1963 and the independent appraisal in 1964. The rent is also shown; that is, the former rent, the new rent and the estimated fair market rent for each type of house. Rather than read this, Mr. Chairman-it would be difficult to follow if I just gave the isolated figures- I should like to table a copy of this tabulation and have it made part of Hansard.

Might I suggest, Mr. Chairman, if the committee is agreeable, that the tabulation referred to by the minister be printed in Hansard at this stage of the minister's remarks.

May I also ask the minister if he has any tabulation of costs and revenues?
Not included in this form. I have it before me and if the hon. member will come into my office I will be glad to show it to him in detail.
I want to see it before the estimates pass.

I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I have extra copies of this sheet for each of the other parties if they wish to have one. The last column is headed "fair market rent", and that is the fair market rent in the opinion of the representative of the Bell-Irving firm who made the appraisal.
Hon. members will see that in each case the new rents are substantially below rental charges in the area.
That is all I wish to say on the subject of the Fraserview veterans' housing project, but I should also like to correct another impression that might have been created by an earlier statement. I am sure the committee will be interested to know that as of September 30 starts of new housing units in Canada were up in 1964 by 10.2 per cent over those reported for the same period in 1963.

May I ask the minister a question at this point? Is he suggesting that the d.b.s. news bulletin is inaccurate?

All I am suggesting is that the figures I am giving may be as of a different date and they may also represent a comparison with a different period. I am comparing the first nine months of 1964 with the corresponding nine months of 1963, and the figures show that starts actually are up by 10.2 per cent.

I think the figures I quoted from the bulletin were for the same period.
I do not have it before me now because I gave it to Hansard, but my recollection is that the figure in the bulletin was as of the same date, September 29, 1964. If d.b.s. is wrong may I suggest there is an obvious lack of accurate communication between C.M.H.C. and d.b.s.

That may be but this is the figure and I am prepared to stand behind it. It is up 10.2 per cent for the first nine months. This means that if the winter housebuilding program meets with the same measure of success it did last year, and this is our expectation based on the applications for loans, housing starts in 1964 will be upward of 155,000 units, or the second highest year in Canada's history.
Which was the highest?

I think it was 1958. Prior to this year the second highest was 1963 which now takes third place. On the basis not only of my visit to Halifax and St. John's and the meetings that took place there, but also of my visit to Saskatoon where in company with the minister of the former government a federal-provincial housing project was opened and discussions were had at that time, as well as of visits that I have made to housing projects in Manitoba and Alberta and more recently to my native province of New Brunswick, I would say that a great deal of interest has been stimulated in housing and urban renewal. The scope of the projects, for instance, in the city of Hamilton, in the city of Windsor and in the city of Saint John is beyond belief. The same applies to cities in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is in the midst of one of its busiest and, I think, most challenging years. There is a lot of educational work to be done, but I believe sincerely that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is an efficient and dedicated organization and I invite the committee's early approval of their very modest estimate.

With regard to the column, "new rent", in the table the minister has given us, I think the minister said in his remarks that one of the factors considered was amortization of the outstanding capital, and the minister referred to a rate of 2| per cent. Is that correct?

Two and a half per cent. It was agreed in the initial stages when these houses were being built for veterans that the investment would be recouped over a period of 50 years at the rate of 2J per cent per year. This policy has been carried through, but when some years later a program of sale was embarked upon factors involving speculation and other things came into the picture and they were taken into consideration in determining market values in the respective areas. If I may leave rents aside for a moment, you will note that so far as the sale price is concerned in no case is the adjusted price higher than the original price. In some cases they are slightly higher than cost but they are not higher than the original price.
That is my next question. The adjusted sales price is less than the original-
No, it is not higher.
It is less, I say. What factors were used in making that adjustment? Was the portion of the rent allocated by C.M.H.C. to depreciation considered?
My information is that it was only one of the factors.
Would that be the major factor in considering adjustment?

I think the major factor was that nobody would have to pay more than the house was worth and the object was to try not to disturb either prices or rentals in the particular areas involved. It is not just a case of being fair to a limited number of veterans, for whom I am sure every government would want to do the best it could. The fact is there are other people to whom the government has to be fair, the people who are paying the taxes that make these projects possible.

The government which objected to subsidizing houses, was really asking the veterans to subsidize veterans' houses in some instances. I object strongly to any party taking one line when it is out of office and an entirely different line when it is in office. I have no intention of delaying the committee for long but there are a few observations I wish to make. Earlier this year

the minister spoke of land assembly projects which come under the control of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I asked the minister several questions at that time and I do not feel I received satisfactory answers to them.
The first question I had in mind is this: Why should land assemblies be set up in direct competition with private developers who are obliged to pay taxes on the property while holding it? I refer to the agreement which was signed with the city of Peterborough. It provides that no municipal tax rate or charge of any nature whatsoever shall be levied by the city while the lots are owned by or on behalf of the corporation. In 1952 the city turned over to the corporation 660 acres of land to develop. Since that day the city has received no tax revenue whatsoever from this property, so in effect the city has been asked to make a direct subsidy. No private developer has ever had such a concession made to him. I consider that the city of Peterborough has lost thousands of dollars in tax revenue over the past 12 years. This arrangement was set up in 1952 but there was no development in the area until 1957. If the present government intends to carry on with land assembly projects it should be asked to share in the cost of trunk services such as sewers, water mains and storm drains and also to bear some of the cost of providing main streets and thoroughfares. It should also be asked to pay its fair share of municipal taxes. All private developers in cities today are required to do this.
Another point I should like to bring out is this: If a city does not wish to carry on a scheme of this type and the property involved has not been developed after 10 or 15 years, the land should revert to the municipality and any moneys owing to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should be paid by the municipality. Why should the corporation be allowed to put its property-on the market to the highest bidder and keep the money for the government of Canada, when the corporation has made no investment in it and taken no risk? The only party which has been stuck for an investment is the city itself.
I feel that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should be careful where they set up land assembly projects. I do not feel they should come into an area, as they did in Peterborough, and sell the municipality a project which is not likely to be completed for 10, 15 or 20 years. This is exactly what
Supply-National Revenue was done in my constituency. I feel the project was too big for the area. It is well planned and it is a subdivision of which any city could be proud. On the other hand it has cost the city many thousands of dollars and I do not think it has cost this government or the provincial government anything. Right now the Peterborough land assembly is short of building lots and the corporation points the finger at the city, blaming the city for not keeping lots available. I know that if the city had received more financial assistance from the corporation it would have been in a better position to keep the lots coming forward.
I should like to ask the minister whether he does not feel projects of this type should share in the cost of the municipal services I mentioned earlier and also whether he does not agree that a municipality wishing to withdraw from such a project should be able to do so without the balance of the property reverting to the corporation, which would then make a substantial gain. I should also like to ask the minister whether he does not believe that land assemblies should be kept for public housing and for the construction of houses for older people and for people with small pensions.
There is one other point I would like to raise before resuming my seat. I think this matter was mentioned by the hon. member for Yukon, but I wish to raise it specifically. It refers to Indians. I believe they should have money available from Central Mortgage and Housing to build on the reserves. I would refer to a young constituent of mine, 25 years old, who came to the city of Peterborough, educated himself and now has a job in the city. He is married and wants to build a house for himself on the Indian reserve, under the provisions of the National Housing Act, and commute to Peterborough. He made application under N.H.A. to build a home on the property owned by him on the reserve, but was refused. I would like to ask the minister if there is not some legislation which would permit those living on Indian reserves to obtain such a loan. This is one way in which we could improve living conditions on reserves. I think the minister and his department should consider these suggestions and look into the possibility of making these loans available to deserving Indians.

subtopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext:
second reading of Bill No. C-43, to amend the Post Office Act (hate literature).
He said: Mr. Speaker, Canadian cities from Montreal to Vancouver in recent months have been inundated by hundreds of thousands of pamphlets, some of them by mail and some by door to door distribution. The material in these pamphlets has been of the kind that most of us thought would have disappeared with the defeat of Hitler's armies in Germany. Much of the material has been actual reprints from material which was published by the nazis in Germany. I am sure hon. members have seen copies of the infamous paper put out by the nazis called Der Sturmer which went to many homes across Canada. I have with me, as I am sure other hon. members have, some samples of the literature which has been distributed. One distributed in Toronto some months ago, which has been referred to in this house on a number of occasions, mailed from Scarborough and printed originally in Atlanta, Georgia, comes from the National White Americans Party. Mr. Speaker, I wish to read just a couple of lines from this pamphlet to indicate the kind of filth which is going into Canadian homes:
(Mr. Mcllraith.]
We believe in sending all negroes back to Africa whence they came. The negro races have never developed a civilization, discovered any new invention, written a great symphony, or even originated an alphabet. They are on a much lower level to the whites.
Coming a couple of days after Martin Luther King received the Nobel prize for work for peace, I think this indicates the level to which such material descends. Later on, the same pamphlet says:
On the Jewish question our policy is much stricter. We demand the arrest of all Jews involved in communist or Zionist plots, public trials and executions. All other Jews would be immediately sterilized so that they could not breed more Jews. This is vital because the Jews are criminals as a race, who have been active in anti-Christian plots throughout their entire history.
Last week in the city of Ottawa I received a pamphlet, apparently printed in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, but mailed in Toronto, headed "Anti-Semitism, a Phony Bogey." Some weeks ago an Ottawa resident sent me a copy of a paper, put out in Ottawa, called The South End News, which is mailed through the facilities of the post office. Its issue of August 6, 1964 devoted a full page to the reprint from the Protocols of Zion, incidentally quoting Henry Ford as to the veracity of it, even though it is well known Mr. Ford made a public statement many years ago saying he realized this was a complete forgery.
This is the kind of material being distributed in Montreal and Toronto. I have also with me a statement issued by the secretary of the B.C. federation of labour, Mr. O'Neal, referring to the kind of material which is being distributed in Vancouver. In my own city of Winnipeg the Winnipeg junior chamber of commerce, in the summer issue of its magazine called Actimist, printed a whole page with a montage of the kind of pamphlets being distributed in Winnipeg.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that in proposing any kind of legislation which would restrict the rights of people in Canada to use the mails, I can be accused of infringing on the democratic rights of people, and that I can be accused of supporting censorship. However, since coming to this house I have consistently defended the rights of any and all groups, no matter what their opinions, no matter how small a minority, to have the widest democratic rights, above all the right to express their opinions. But it seems to me we must distinguish between democratic rights and licence, licence to incite to vio-

lence, licence to incite to kill, licence to attack people on the basis of race, creed, colour or religion.
For those of us who were born in Canada and who have lived under a democratic system of society, most of us looking at this kind of material would think it was ridiculous that it could not have any effect and that we ought to ignore it. But that was precisely the attitude taken by so many people in Germany, until it was too late.
A large number of organizations have called on the government to take action in respect to this matter. I am sure the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) know better than I do the organizations which have written them and which have passed resolutions urging action on this matter. I have seen some of the material. I have seen editorials, written in newspapers published in almost every city of Canada, calling on the government to take action.
I know that the Canadian Legion passed resolutions at its national convention. I know that the Canadian Labour Congress submitted a brief to the Minister of Justice calling for action. I know that the Canadian Jewish Congress has called for amendments to the Criminal Code. Just briefly I wish to refer to two of these submissions made to the government, in order to indicate the kind of proposals which the government has been asked to consider.
The Canadian Labour Congress, in a brief presented to the Minister of Justice on April 7, 1964, by the president of the congress, Mr. Claude Jodoin, made two specific recommendations, and I quote:
We call upon the government to enact legislation which would require the authors, publishers, distributors and printers of any printed matter being sent through the mails to identify themselves clearly on the face of the material which they disseminate. This legislation should be drafted in such a way as to require the identification of at least one responsible officer as well as that of the organization itself. It should also identify the Canadian accomplices in the distribution of materials printed outside of Canada.
If such a proposal had been adopted by the government it would in fact only be applying to this kind of material the same kind of provisions which we have in our legislation with respect to elections, which require that all election material have the person responsible for its printing identified on it. In fact it is similar to the kind of provisions which are in the labour relations
Private Bills
act, which require a union, during an organizing campaign, to identify itself on any printed material it distributes.
The Canadian Labour Congress in its brief also said:
We call upon the government to enact legislation making it illegal to publish statements which are designed to incite violence or disorder against groups because of the group's race, creed, colour, place of birth, national or ethnic origin.
On March 12, 1964 the Canadian Jewish Congress submitted a brief to the Minister of Justice and the Postmaster General, in which they made several specific proposals, one being that section 166(2) of the Criminal Code include the following:
Injury or mischief to a public interest shall include the promotion of hatred, contempt or hostility against a group of persons by reason of their particular race, national or ethnic origin, colour or religion.
And that a new section 62A should read:
Every person who publishes or circulates or causes to be published or circulated, orally or in writing, any matter or statement which is intended or calculated to incite violence or disorder against a group of persons of a particular race, national or ethnic origin, colour or religion, or against the members thereof, shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable for imprisonment for two years.
I know that both these briefs received very sympathetic consideration from the Minister of Justice. I know he is concerned, and rightly so, about the kind of hate literature which is being distributed. Nevertheless he and his officials have not been able to draft legislation which, though not accepting the specific proposals I have quoted, would at least begin to meet some of the problems which have arisen. It is for that reason I hope the house will give serious consideration to my bill today.
I recognize there may be difficulties. I recognize that once you begin to put any kind of prohibition on the freest dissemination of printed material you may run into difficulty. But, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that until the government brings in alternative legislation, which the Minister of Justice on a number of occasions has indicated the government is considering, the house should give sympathetic and favourable consideration to my proposal.
My proposal is a very simple one. It is merely an addition to section 7 of the Post Office Act, which would spell out the rights of the Postmaster General to restrict the mailing rights of people who are using the mails to distribute hate literature.
On Wednesday of this week, as reported at page 9041 of Hansard, the minister was

Private Bills
asked a question by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker), with respect to actions which he had taken in several cases. The minister made an excellent statement to the effect that he had already taken action against several people who had been found responsible for the dissemination of hate literature. I think the actions of the minister were very proper and very correct. I am concerned, however, that should he take similar action in the future his orders might be challenged, not simply before a board of review, which I understand is an internal organization, but on the basis that the hon. gentleman does not have the power under the Post Office Act as it now stands to issue orders of the kind he has already made.
The gist of my bill is simply to spell out the legislation so that there may be no question that the minister has the right to take action to remove mailing privileges from people who disseminate literature of this kind. As I said earlier, those of us who were born in Canada and who have lived here all our lives may not regard this as a very important matter. We may not feel that many people will be misled by this kind of filth which has been widely disseminated. However, to the people who have come from Europe, more than a million of them, from countries where literature of this kind was extensively used to divide people, this is a matter which is serious, which really is urgent, and in respect of which the government should take action and take action now.

subtopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext:
Let me say at the outset of my remarks that nobody in this chamber is more disgusted or more shocked than I am at the distribution of the vicious material of the kind referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).
To me it makes no difference whether this vile material is distributed through the mail or by any other means; it is offensive and objectionable and every reasonable effort must be made to stop it. Nobody is more anxious than I, or the government, to put an end to this filthy business and to protect the innocent persons in Canada who have suffered from such conduct.
As I have stated more than once in this house, my department is working closely with the Department of Justice in an effort not only to find some effective legislation to deal with this situation, but to find an effective means of applying existing laws to cut off what I think has properly been referred to as traffic in hate. We are trying to find a means of amending the law in a way which

will accomplish the purpose the hon. member had in mind when he introduced this bill.
I will admit frankly, however, that in searching for a solution to this problem we are on the horns of a dilemma. If, on the other hand, we do not take effective action against these nefarious traffickers in hate literature, this traffic is likely to continue. On the other hand, and this is what distresses me-and I know it distresses others with whom I have discussed it-if we do take strict measures to shut off the use of the mails to those who deal in hate literature we shall almost certainly prejudice the rights and freedom of the majority of Canadians and others who use our mails for decent and legitimate purposes.
Perhaps we should look back on history. It will be recalled that the privacy of the royal mails has always by law and practice been sacrosanct, at any rate in this country. In times of peace post office officials have never had the right to act as censors, to open deliverable letters and, more important, to decide what is objectionable or unacceptable correspondence. I believe that we in this house must make very sure that any action we may take to suppress the transmission of hate literature is not likely to result in a situation where government officials, with no trained jurists to guide them-and certainly the officials of my department are not trained jurists-would be called upon to exercise censorship of the mails and to impose their ideas of morality upon the public at large. I believe that legislation which would permit such a situation would be striking a blow at the very roots of our freedom of speech and expression. If today we decide it is illegal to express an opinion about a religious sect or group, then tomorrow why should we not make it illegal to attack a political party or to question the authority of the government? If there is one thing I have learned in the few months I have been Postmaster General, it is that the post office is really a service organization; it is in the business of carrying the mails expeditiously. It is not our responsibility or our business to decide what opinions are legal or illegal. Surely that is a matter for the courts. And when the courts have made the decisions as to what is right or wrong and what should or should not be distributed, then I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, the post office will exert every reasonable effort to carry that decision into effect when it has to do with the use of Her Majesty's mails.

Private Bills
I am well aware that certain sections of the Post Office Act and of the Criminal Code give the Postmaster General the authority to prohibit the use of the mails for illegal purposes and, as has just been mentioned by the hon. member for Winnpeg North, I have had occasion to exercise my powers under that statute more than once during the last few months. Twice I have issued orders, once in July and again in late September, under section 7 of the act under which I have been given the right, if I feel that a section of the Criminal Code is being broken, to prohibit the use of the mail for the distribution of indecent or scurrilous literature. I had no doubt about reaching the conclusion that the material in question was scurrilous and I had no hesitation in imposing these orders, the first of which now stands as a final order.
Obviously, however, an attempt has been made to get around my first order because directly it was put into effect another organization, with a name similar to the one I had prohibited, came into being. That is what happens in these cases. The organizations affected go under cover, adopt a new name and start out afresh. However, I have not hesitated to use my authority where I can in an effort to suppress the distribution of scurrilous literature whether by organizations or by individuals. We will block it in Canada, and we will block it coming into Canada if we have to.
In the last case-and the literature to which the hon. member has just referred is this type of literature-the literature was so vicious, so outrageous, so scurrilous that I felt I had very firm grounds for taking the action that I did. But I should point out and reiterate what I said a moment ago, that what has happened in this particular case illustrates the thing about which I am most concerned, namely that it drives these people underground and they seek the protection and privacy of the first class mail, which we cannot open. We cannot under such circumstances even perform the service we are performing now, if they resort to that practice. When this happens we have a very limited course of action open to us.
My department and the Department of Justice have this difficult problem under active and intensive study. We have not as yet, unfortunately, come up with what we consider to be an effective solution-that is to say, a solution that would stop the flow of hate literature but at the same time would not interfere with the right of free expression
or the privacy-and this is what concerns us -of the mails. If we had to open all letters in trying to find out whether or not hate literature or even vicious material was being distributed, we would come across all kinds of secrets and we would find ourselves acting as censors in many fields which are of no concern to the department.
It is my opinion that if a solution-and we must strive to find a solution-is to be found, it will lie in an amendment to the Criminal Code or some similar statute, rather than in changes in the Post Office Act. I say this because, as I intimated earlier, in my opinion-and I practised law for nearly 20 years before I went into business, and had some experience in the criminal courts as well as with constitutional law-the courts, which interpret the Criminal Code and our other statutes, are the logical persons, are the proper judges, of what literature is decent, what literature is vicious, what literature is legal and what literature is illegal. In my humble opinion it is not for post office officials to make such decisions, as I am sure most members of this house will agree.
Mr. Speaker, from the time the first newspaper was printed and the first broadside distributed, those whose views were offended have cried out for control, for censorship. It is easy to say, "This material is vicious," or "scurrilous," or "poisonous. Ban it from the mails". But I again say, who is to judge what is vicious, what is scurrilous and what is poisonous, unless it can be brought to the attention of some person charged with the specific responsibility, and brought before that person in a proper way? Especially, who is to make the decision as to just what sealed letters officials of the post office can open? If they do, what do you do with mail that comes in a plain envelope, first class mail? It will be said that some of the cases that have been discussed in the house, including some of those mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), this afternoon are very obviously scurrilous. I most certainly agree. But if we start, where do we stop? Do we prohibit the use of the mails to a newspaper because it attacks a political organization? Do we ban the use of mails to those religious publications that violently and intolerantly oppose other denominations?
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I loathe and detest the foul propaganda that has been circulated throughout this country by people with warped and twisted minds. I believe that every possible action should be taken against them under the law. But in saying that, Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Private Bills
Speaker, let us make sure that we do not set up a machine that is perhaps potentially more dangerous than the evil we are fighting. Let us make sure that the medicine is not worse than the disease. Let us make sure that our decisions as to what is right and what is wrong are made by the established process of law, by the courts, and not by officials of the post office or any other department. They certainly should not be made by persons whose prime job is to distribute the mail as quickly and as expeditiously as possible. They are not there to act as censors; they are there to do the job in the quickest and most expeditious way.

subtopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, have received some of the literature that the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has described. I think all members of this house join in agreeing that it is offensive, that it is deplorable that persons should take it upon themselves, first of all to write and then to distribute this kind of despicable material. I think too that when we understand that there is an opportunity, through paying a certain amount of postage, to deliver these things through the mail to a great many people who have not subscribed to them, they do take offence and resent the fact that this kind of material is being sent into their homes.
I have to agree, however, with the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) that there are some very serious problems involved in administering the provisions contained in Bill No. C-43. The minister mentioned-and I was pleased that he did mention these things- that a post office department is not and should not be a censorship bureau or organization; they are primarily, and perhaps even solely, concerned with being a service organization to deliver the mail. Therefore we run into the problem, because I do not see it provided for in the amendments to the act that are proposed to us, of who is going to decide what is in fact calculated to bring into hatred, ridicule or contempt any person or group of persons by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion. It is, as has been quite properly stated, a matter for the courts to decide as to what should be calculated to bring into hatred or ridicule any of these things.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this is not an easy matter. I think it is well that we have this bill before us so we may discuss this problem, cast some light on it and then give consideration to what can be done about it.

As has been said by both hon. members who have spoken, it is an offensive thing to receive some of these pieces of literature, but at the same time to amend the Post Office Act in such a way that you can prevent this literature being carried is perhaps not the way to deal with it. I think, too, that the Criminal Code should be amended so it could be made substantially more clear with regard to what would be an offence, to be decided by the courts, with regard to printing this kind of literature. But I do not think members of the house would be satisfied to set up any quasi judicial committee or board to really decide whether an offence had been committed, because the two or three pieces of literature from which the hon. member for Winnipeg North quoted are certainly extreme cases and there would be no problem in deciding that this was scurrilous, offensive, and so on. If we were to write into the statutes the provision that this be decided by the Post Office Department, they are certainly going to be presented with other pieces of literature not so extreme. Then it will be a problem of making a decision whether or not they are an offence under the act.
I want to join with the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) in expressing our distaste at the fact that it is possible for this sort of thing to be distributed; but at the same time I believe we must be pretty careful about charging the Post Office Department with a responsibility with which they are not equipped to deal, and further must be reasonably careful not to set up restrictions in the use of mail which really may not serve the purpose for which they are designed.

subtopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) for the action he took in July and September of this year in passing judgment on this scurrilous literature and I believe he has earned the approval of every right thinking man, certainly in this house and in the Dominion of Canada.
It is not my purpose to deal with this matter at length but I should like to bring to the attention of the house a statement made by President Johnson after the assassination of President Kennedy. It is printed by the Institute of Human Relations of the United States and the quotation is as follows:
The time has come for Americans of all races and creeds and political beliefs to understand and to respect one another. So, let us put an end to the teaching and preaching of hate and evil and

violence. Let us turn away from the fanatics, from the far left and the far right, from the apostles of bitterness and bigotry, from those defiant of law, and those who pour venom into our nation's bloodstream.
Appearing in the Montreal Star of this week is an article dealing with the appearance of President Johnson in Corpus Christi, Texas, this Sunday. A raid had been made by the police and an ex-plumber was questioned, at whose home the police seized guns and nazi flags in connection with a reported plot to kill President Johnson this Sunday. The police chief and 25 deputies gathered up machine guns, automatic pistols, high-powered rifles, a mortar, a rocket launcher, live hand grenades and about 20,000 rounds of commercial and homemade ammunition, swords, several nazi flags, world war I and II German helmets, and so on. I bring this to the attention of the house in order to indicate that hate literature brings the kind of violence it breeds, especially in the state of Texas. Because where hate literature flourishes it creates an atmosphere which gives the assassin the courage which he would not have in a healthy and sane community.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house the fact that in discussing another bill dealing with group defamation there was a motion to send it to the external affairs committee as set out in the motion at page 5984 of Hansard. I would be happy to have this bill referred to that committee, since the motion stood in the name of the government, and particularly since the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), at page 7823 of Hansard, is reported as saying:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this question of hate literature and the action to be taken under the Criminal Code has been under consideration by the government for months, would the minister consider setting up a special committee of the house to look into the whole problem, to hear the law officers of the crown, and to ascertain whether action has been taken in other parts of the world without interference with freedom, to the end that the house might favour the recommendation of amendments to the Criminal Code-
And so on. In view of the fact that the government seems to favour a committee for this type of subject matter, whether the external affairs committee or some other committee, and in view of the fact that the Leader of the Opposition, and I believe the leaders of other parties also favour committee consideration, I hope that a clinical study can be made of this bill by referring it and all other bills of this nature to that committee.

subtopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) for the worth-while initiative he took in introducing Bill No. C-43 to amend section 7 of the Post Office Act.
Before proceeding with my remarks on this bill, I feel it would be proper to read section 7 of the Post Office Act:
(1) Whenever the Postmaster General believes on reasonable grounds that any person
(a)	is, by means of the mails,
(i)	committing or attempting to commit an offence, or
(ii)	aiding, counselling or procuring any person to commit an offence, or
(b)	with intent to commit an offence, is using the mails for the purpose of accomplishing his object, the Postmaster General may make an interim order (in this section called an "interim prohibitory order") prohibiting the delivery of all mail directed to that person (in this section called the "person affected") or deposited by that person in a post office.
The amendment provided for in Bill No. C-43 apparently would deny in effect the use of Her Majesty's mail to persons who address or disseminate hate literature calculated to foster hatred, cast contempt or ridicule on any person or group of persons for reasons of race, national origin, colour, religion, etc.
This matter, Mr. Speaker, has been brought up in this house many times before, and I entirely agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North who, with all his deep and sincere feelings, respects the rights and freedoms of every citizen of this country, whatever his tongue, religion, nationality or colour.
I am one of those who in this house have vehemently protested against the almost systematic poisoning of our youth and our whole population, as practised by certain publicity media in this country. The mails, Mr. Speaker, are not the only means used for discriminatory purposes. One only has to read certain newspapers and publications and look at certain television programs to realize the immense harm and sometimes irretrievable injury which some of those writings, programs or broadcasts can inflict upon the individual, the family and the Canadian population in general.
